To return to the hyperlink location after navigating, press the ALT + left arrow keys on your keyboard. 2. This summary is specifically designed for nonclinical providers who work in community-based organizations or health departments outside of healthcare facilities. These providers deliver services such as HIV testing, health education, risk reduction interventions, partner services, case management, and assistance with linkage or referral to medical and social services. 3. The 2014 guideline, titled Recommendations for HIV Prevention with Adults and Adolescents with HIV in the United States, includes updated federal guidance on biomedical, behavioral, and structural interventions aimed at reducing HIV transmission by decreasing infectiousness and exposure risk. It builds upon earlier guidance from 2003, which focused on incorporating HIV prevention into the medical care of individuals living with HIV. 4. The 2014 guideline and this summary were developed collaboratively by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), the National Institutes of Health (NIH), and other professional organizations such as the American Academy of HIV Medicine and the Association of Nurses in AIDS Care. 5. This summary includes recommendations for 11 domains of interventions that can reduce HIV transmission by lowering the infectiousness of individuals with HIV or reducing their risk of exposing others. It also provides practical strategies for implementation, links to federal guidance, and access to an online resource library. 6. Nonclinical providers can use this summary to learn how they and their organizations can promote HIV prevention, select appropriate interventions for their clients, and train staff on best practices in HIV prevention. 7. Sustained high adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART) is critical for improving clinical outcomes, quality of life, and reducing the risk of HIV transmission. Nonclinical providers can support ART adherence by collaborating with clinical providers, offering counseling, training on medication reminder tools, and providing case management services. 8. Nonclinical providers can play a vital role in informing clients about the benefits of early ART initiation, supporting long-term adherence, and providing information on interventions to reduce HIV transmission risk. They can also educate clients about prophylactic medications for their HIV-uninfected partners when clinically indicated. 9. Nonclinical providers can assist in partner services by counseling individuals with HIV about disclosure, collecting partner contact information, and offering HIV testing to partners. In some jurisdictions, trained and authorized nonclinical providers can deliver partner services in community-based HIV testing and prevention programs. 10. STD preventive services are essential for individuals with HIV, as certain STDs can increase the risk of HIV transmission. Nonclinical providers can assess risk factors, provide sexual risk reduction information, and link clients to STD screening and treatment services. 11. Reproductive healthcare for individuals with HIV includes services to prevent unplanned pregnancies and reduce the risk of sexual HIV transmission during conception. Nonclinical providers can provide education, referrals, and support for these services, including linking clients to providers familiar with special conception methods. 12. Pregnant women with HIV can transmit the virus to their fetuses or newborns if effective prevention strategies are not used. Nonclinical providers can offer preventive services, link pregnant women to HIV care, and provide HIV testing to pregnant women and their partners. 13. Nonclinical providers should inform women and their partners that breastfeeding by HIV-infected women is not recommended in the United States, and formula feeding is advised for their infants. 14. Nonclinical providers can support adherence to ART during prenatal and postnatal periods, offer condoms, and assist women in notifying their partners about their HIV status. However, explicit permission from the woman is required to discuss her HIV status with her partners. 15. Nonclinical providers can also provide education and referrals for postpartum contraception services to women who wish to prevent or delay future pregnancies.
